prompt: In pull_push.py, why does the line "Iracema is back" never appear in the pull half?

choices.text: The generator raised an error on the third title and the loop swallowed it
choices.why: Nothing raised; the transcript shows no error, and a for loop does not swallow exceptions.

choices.text: Nobody asked for a third book
choices.why: Right. A generator runs only as far as the next value somebody requests, and islice stopped after two.

choices.text: The desk printed it, but after the push half had started, so it scrolled away
choices.why: The output is in order and complete; the push half prints its own three lines about the desk.

prompt: Match each way of getting values to what gives you them.
Which of these sources is a poor fit for pulling, so that a reactive design suits it?

choices.text: A CSV file of last year's loans, read row by row
choices.why: A file waits for the next read; an ordinary loop over it is simpler and never holds more than it asked for.

choices.text: A database cursor over the members table
choices.why: A cursor fetches when asked, so the consumer can set the pace, which is the strength of pull.

choices.text: Messages arriving on a socket from the self-service kiosks
choices.why: Right. The kiosks send when a member uses them; the program cannot ask them to wait, which is the case push exists for.

choices.text: A list of titles already in memory
choices.why: Everything is there before you start; looping over it is pull at its simplest.

prompt: returns = of("Dom Casmurro", "Vidas Secas") runs, and nothing else yet. What has been printed by the observable?

choices.text: Nothing: no one has subscribed
choices.why: Right. An observable is a description; the producer runs inside subscribe.

choices.text: Both titles, because of() pushes its values as soon as it is called
choices.why: of() only builds an Observable around a producer; the transcript prints "built; nothing has happened yet" first.

choices.text: The first title, held until a subscriber arrives
choices.why: Nothing is held: there is no buffer in Observable, only a function waiting to be called.

prompt: The careless producer calls on_next("O Cortiço") after on_complete(). Why does the subscriber never see it?

choices.text: Python stops a function at the first call to a method named on_complete
choices.why: The producer keeps running; the call happens and the sink decides what to do with it.

choices.text: The sink closed at the completion and ignores every later signal
choices.why: Right. The rule about endings is kept by Sink for every producer, so no producer has to remember it.

choices.text: Titles are deduplicated, and O Cortiço was already sent
choices.why: Nothing deduplicates, and O Cortiço had not been sent; the producer sent Iracema before completing.

choices.text: subscribe returned before the producer could send it
choices.why: The producer runs entirely inside subscribe, synchronously; it did send it, to a closed sink.

prompt: A stream sends any number of values, then at most one ending: on_error or on____ , never both.
In the run of operators.py, what is printed immediately after "source: Vidas Secas, 3 days late"?

choices.text: "source: Iracema, 0 days late", because the source sends all four before the operators run
choices.why: That is how three list comprehensions would behave. A stream sends each value down the whole chain first.

choices.text: "fines so far: 150 cents"
choices.why: Right. The value goes through filter_, map_ and scan before the source moves on.

choices.text: "fines so far: 3 cents", because scan runs before map_
choices.why: The operators run in the order written in pipe: filter_, then map_, then scan.

prompt: A fifth return is added to operators.py after O Cortiço: ("Senhora", 2). What is the last running total printed, in cents?
fines = Observable(produce).pipe(filter_(...), map_(...), scan(...)) runs. What has happened to the source?

choices.text: It ran once, and the results are cached for the first subscriber
choices.why: There is no cache anywhere in the chain; each subscription runs the source again.

choices.text: It ran as far as filter_ and is waiting
choices.why: Nothing ran at all, not even the source; pipe only nests one description in another.

choices.text: Nothing has run yet; pipe only built a description
choices.why: Right. Subscribing to fines is what runs the subscriptions upstream and starts the source.

prompt: In the hot half of hot_cold.py, what is the first title Bia sees?

choices.text: Dom Casmurro, replayed to her when she subscribes
choices.why: A plain Subject keeps no history; replaying is what ReplaySubject adds.

choices.text: Vidas Secas, the next title after she joined
choices.why: Right. She joined after Dom Casmurro went past, and a hot stream sends only what happens from then on.

choices.text: None: a subscriber that joins late receives nothing at all
choices.why: Joining late costs only what was already sent; Bia receives the next two titles.

prompt: Which of these sources are hot? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Key presses in the search box of the catalogue page
choices.why: Right. The user types whether or not anything is listening.

choices.text: An HTTP request for the list of new acquisitions
choices.why: Each subscription sends its own request, which is the cold behaviour that surprises people who subscribe twice.

choices.text: Scans from the barcode reader at the returns desk
choices.why: Right. Books pass under the reader on their own schedule.

choices.text: of("Dom Casmurro", "Iracema")
choices.why: of() runs its producer for every subscriber from the first value, which is the definition of cold.

prompt: A page shows the member's loans in two places, and the server log shows two identical requests per page view. What is the likely fix?

choices.text: Make the server answer faster, so that the second request finds the first one's cache
choices.why: Speed does not change how many times a cold observable runs; there would still be two requests.

choices.text: Share one subscription to the request between both places on that page
choices.why: Right. The request is cold, so each subscriber starts its own; an operator such as share makes it one run with two listeners.

choices.text: Turn the request into a Subject that the page pushes values into
choices.why: A Subject is hot, but somebody still has to make the request and push the answer; share does that wiring for you.

choices.text: Unsubscribe the second place as soon as the first one gets its answer
choices.why: By then both requests have been sent; the second place would also show nothing.

prompt: Values arrive faster than they are handled, on average, all day, and an unbounded queue sits between. What happens?

choices.text: The queue and each value's wait keep growing until memory runs out
choices.why: Right. A queue absorbs a burst, never a rate; flood.py's oldest scan was already five seconds old after ten.

choices.text: The queue smooths the rate out, so values are handled late but the backlog stays level
choices.why: It stays level only if the average rate in equals the rate out; flood.py grows by three every second.

choices.text: Python raises queue.Full once the queue reaches its default size
choices.why: An unbounded queue has no size to reach; queue.Full exists only when maxsize is set.

prompt: In flood.py, scans arrive at 5 a second and the catalogue handles 2. How many scans are waiting after 20 seconds?
A Reactive Streams subscriber calls request(1) after handling each value. What does that give it that blocking.py gets by blocking a thread?

choices.text: Values in a guaranteed order, which a queue cannot promise
choices.why: queue.Queue is first in, first out; blocking.py handled all twelve in order.

choices.text: A producer that never sends more than the subscriber said it could take
choices.why: Right. Demand is the same backpressure without a waiting thread: the publisher holds its next value until a request arrives.

choices.text: A way to make the barcode scanner at the desk read more slowly
choices.why: Demand works only when the producer can hold back; the scanner cannot, which is why section 07 exists.

choices.text: Lost values counted automatically by the library
choices.why: With demand nothing is lost; counting losses belongs to the drop and latest strategies.

prompt: Match each kind of data to the strategy the section recommends for a full queue.

pairs.left: loans being returned at the desk
pairs.right: block, or a bounded buffer with an alarm

pairs.left: copies of a book on the shelf, sent on every change
page views for a weekly report

prompt: In strategies.py, drop and latest each handled about a third of the scans. What does latest give that drop does not?

choices.text: It loses fewer scans
choices.why: It loses more: eight against drop's seven.

choices.text: The catalogue always works on the newest scan, ending with scan 12
choices.why: Right. Drop keeps the old scans and throws the new ones away, so its last handled scan is 10 and scan 12 is lost.

choices.text: A queue that can hold more than two scans when it needs to
choices.why: Latest holds one at most; growing past the capacity is what buffer does.

prompt: Block and buffer both handled all twelve scans and finished at tick 36. Where did block put the cost that buffer kept in memory?

choices.text: Nowhere: block is simply the better strategy
choices.why: The difference between the rates has to go somewhere, and block only works on a producer that can wait.

choices.text: In lost scans, counted in the lost column
choices.why: Block lost none; its lost column is 0, like buffer's.

choices.text: In the producer's time: the scanner finished at tick 31 instead of 12
choices.why: Right. The difference between the two rates has to live somewhere: in a growing queue, or in a producer that waits.

prompt: Why does RxJS have no request(n), when Reactor builds everything on it?

choices.text: JavaScript is single-threaded, so a producer can never be faster than its consumer
choices.why: One thread does not stop events piling up; that is why RxJS ships throttleTime and sampleTime.

choices.text: Most browser sources are hot and cannot be slowed, so it offers lossy operators instead
choices.why: Right. A user does not click more slowly because a handler is busy.

choices.text: It was written before Reactive Streams existed and has not caught up
choices.why: The section says it was decided on purpose: demand would have little to slow down in a browser.

prompt: In Go, a send to a buffered channel is wrapped in select with a default case that increments dropped. Which strategy is that?

choices.text: block, because channels always block
choices.why: A plain send blocks; default runs exactly when the send would have to wait.

choices.text: latest, because the newest scan replaces the one in the channel
choices.why: Nothing is taken out of the channel; the new scan is the one that goes.

choices.text: drop, counted
choices.why: Right. When the channel is full, the new scan is discarded, and the counter makes the loss visible.

choices.text: buffer, because the channel was made with a capacity
choices.why: The capacity is a bound; an unbounded buffer would never reach the default case.

prompt: fines.subscribe(...) is called in operators.py. Put what happens in order.
items: scan's producer subscribes to the observable map_ returned
map_'s producer subscribes to filter_'s observable
filter_'s producer subscribes to the source
The source pushes Dom Casmurro into filter_'s callback
Vidas Secas reaches the subscriber as 150
trap: Subscriptions run upstream, from the end of the chain to the source, before any value comes down.

prompt: A screen in the reading room shows how many study desks are free, from a sensor stream that changes many times a minute. Screens are switched on at any time of day. Which design fits?

choices.text: A cold observable that reads the sensors from the start for every screen, with a buffer so no change is lost
choices.why: The sensors are hot and the past is worthless here; buffering every change only makes the screen show old counts.

choices.text: Hot, holding the current value for any newcomer, and latest for anyone who falls behind
choices.why: Right. Like a BehaviorSubject: a screen switched on at noon needs the count now, and only the newest count matters.

choices.text: A plain Subject, and block so that the sensors wait for the slowest screen
choices.why: A plain Subject gives a late screen nothing until the next change, and sensors cannot be made to wait.

prompt: Fine payments arrive from the bank as events, sometimes in bursts of hundreds. The handler records each one in the database. Which choice is wrong here?

choices.text: Latest, so the handler always works on the newest payment
choices.why: Right, that is the wrong one. A payment is a fact: replacing one with the next loses money a member really paid.

choices.text: A bounded buffer with an alarm when it fills
choices.why: That one is sound: bursts end, nothing is lost, and the alarm says when they do not.

choices.text: Demand, if the bank's interface lets the handler ask for payments in batches
choices.why: That one is sound too: when the producer can hold back, letting the consumer set the pace loses nothing.
